summary: On 21 June 2022 a resilience project changed prefix advertisement policy in Cloudflare's busiest locations. A reordered term withdrew critical prefixes, taking 19 data centers, about half of requests, offline for over an hour.

overview.background: Cloudflare was rolling out a change for its Multi-Colo PoP (MCP) architecture in 19 data centers, which are about 4 percent of its network but handle about half of requests.
overview.impact: Users in affected regions could not reach sites relying on Cloudflare from 06:27 to about 07:42 UTC. Other regions were unaffected.
overview.severity: Large, roughly 75 minutes. Cloudflare says it was its own error, not an attack.
overview.gaps: The post gives no request counts.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: A reordered term rejects site-local prefixes
diagrams.caption: A reject term ended up before the site-local terms, so those prefixes were withdrawn. The internal load balancer went down and smaller clusters overloaded.

nodes.label: Policy terms reordered: reject before site-local
Internal load balancer off, compute clusters overload

edges.label: stagger skipped MCP until the end

diagrams.title: Staged rollout with auto-rollback (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Cloudflare planned MCP-specific testing, stronger staggered rollout and automated commit-confirm rollback. This picture shows the idea.

afterChanges: MCP sites are tested like others.
A bad change rolls back automatically.

timeline.e: The change is deployed to a first location, which is unaffected because it uses the older architecture.
The change reaches the busiest locations, but not the MCP sites.
The rollout reaches MCP sites and spines. The incident begins, taking 19 locations offline.
A first router change is made to verify the root cause.
The root cause is identified and the revert begins. The first data center returns.

rootCause.trigger: A prefix advertisement policy update reordered terms in the MCP locations.
rootCause.underlying: The reject term sat ahead of the site-local terms, so critical prefixes were withdrawn.
contributing: The stagger policy did not include MCP sites until the last step
The 19 locations handled about half of requests
Engineers' conflicting changes slowed the revert and reintroduced the problem briefly

evidence.label: Ownership
evidence.body: This was our error and not the result of an attack or malicious activity.

evidence.label: The mechanism
evidence.body: a re-ordering of terms caused us to withdraw a critical subset of prefixes.

evidence.label: A simulated policy ordering
evidence.body:
term 1: from site-local-prefixes then accept
term 2: from backbone-prefixes then accept
term 99: then reject
evidence.note: Illustrates why a reject term must come last. Generic syntax, invented.

diagnose.step: Check what changed in the first affected locations.
diagnose.why: A change had just reached MCP.

diagnose.step: Check which prefixes are advertised from the sites.
diagnose.why: Missing site-local prefixes explained the outage.

diagnose.step: Check whether load balancers and clusters are healthy.

correct.why: The revert restored sites one by one.

correct.step: Coordinate engineers so changes do not conflict.

verify.step: Check traffic and load per site.
verify.why: Confirm clusters are no longer overloaded.

prevent.step: Redesign policy to prevent unintended term order.

fix.safety: Several engineers changing one device during recovery can undo each other. Assign one owner per device.

troubleshoot.scenario: A router policy change just reached your busiest sites. Half of requests fail and site prefixes disappeared.
troubleshoot.question: What is your plan?
troubleshoot.answer: Revert the policy using out-of-band access with a single owner per device, confirm prefixes are advertised, then add term-order tests and staged rollout.

rootcause.q: How many data centers were hit?

remediation.answer: Check that every site-local prefix is accepted by the final policy.
Include one MCP site in the first stage.

design.prompt: Design a network change process for sites that carry half of traffic.
design.answer: Treat the biggest sites as separate classes with their own tests, small first stages, and automatic rollback.

checks.q: What share of the network were the 19 locations?
checks.why: They handled about 50 percent of requests.

checks.q: What was wrong with the policy?
options: A reject term sat before the site-local terms
